facts.fact: The rational numbers have the same cardinality as the natural numbers.
facts.note: Correct. This sets up the contrast with the reals.

facts.fact: Mathematicians call any infinite set that matches the natural numbers countable.
facts.note: Strictly this is 'countably infinite'. 'Countable' also includes finite sets. The brief's wording is acceptable.

facts.fact: Cantor assumed a complete list of all real numbers between zero and one.
facts.note: This is a proof by contradiction.

facts.fact: He created a new decimal number by altering each digit along the diagonal.
facts.note: Correct.

facts.fact: The new number differs from the nth listed number at the nth decimal digit.
facts.note: Correct.

facts.fact: The new decimal cannot exist anywhere on the supposedly complete list.
facts.note: Correct. The brief does not mention that digits must be chosen to avoid 0.4999... = 0.5000... duplicates, for example by using only 4s and 5s.

facts.fact: This contradiction proves that no complete list of real numbers is possible.
facts.note: Correct.

facts.fact: The real numbers form an uncountable infinite set.
facts.note: Correct.

facts.fact: Cantor showed that real numbers have a strictly larger cardinality than natural numbers.
facts.note: Correct. This is the central answer to the reader's goal.

facts.fact: Cantor's theorem shows that the power set of any set has a strictly larger cardinality.
facts.note: Correct. It shows there are infinitely many sizes of infinity. 'Power set' is not explained.

facts.fact: Cantor's paradox demonstrates that no largest cardinal number exists.
facts.note: Correct. It follows from Cantor's theorem, and it is a bit advanced for a new reader.

accuracy.why: Every fact is true. The only imprecision is that 'countable' is used for 'countably infinite'.

clarity.why: The sentences are short and plain. Some terms such as power set and cardinal number are not defined.

coverage.why: The brief covers the core argument. It lacks a concrete pairing example, an example of the diagonal construction, the symbols ℵ₀ and 2^ℵ₀, and the intuition for the power set. It also has no mention of Hilbert's Hotel or of 'bigger' meaning no pairing is possible.

currency.why: This is settled mathematics. Nothing here changes with time.

decisions.why: Subject kind, quick format and 3 chapters suit a new reader with one idea. Three chapters is a little tight for the content.

framing.why: The line is specific and natural. 'In one quick read' is a bit formulaic.

goalFit.why: Most facts go straight to why some infinities are bigger. Cantor's paradox is slightly advanced, and the 1891 date adds little.

sources.why: The sources are real and relevant: two Wikipedia pages, an HMC page and a Medium article. All are reasonable for a beginner, but none is a primary or textbook source.

specificity.why: The statements are checkable but abstract. There are no worked examples, such as a short list with a diagonal digit change.

verdict.worst: The brief gives only abstract statements, with no worked examples or intuition, so the writer has little concrete material for a beginner.

A's pgvector 'fifty million vectors' figure is a specific claim that may be overstated, which is a minor risk.
